candidates.label: Sardis archaeological site (Sart)
candidates.support: The extensively excavated site near modern Sart is undisputed as ancient Sardis, capital of the Kingdom of Lydia; Pleiades and Wikidata's coordinates for the site agree closely.

summary.text: Sardis stood at the foot of Mount Tmolus, on the edge of the fertile Hermus river plain, combining a steep, naturally fortified acropolis with a much larger lower city on the plain below. It had been the capital of the ancient kingdom of Lydia, whose king Croesus became proverbial for his wealth, drawn partly from gold dust carried down from Mount Tmolus by the small Pactolus river, until the Persian conquest of 547/546 BC. By Paul's day it was a major city of the Roman province of Asia. In AD 17 a catastrophic earthquake struck twelve cities of Asia in a single night; the Roman historian Tacitus records that Sardis suffered the worst damage of them all and received the largest relief from the emperor Tiberius, a ten-million-sesterce grant and a five-year tax remission.

history.text: Sardis is one of the seven churches addressed in Revelation, rebuked there for having "a reputation of being alive," though "you are dead," and warned, "I will come as a thief, and you won't know what hour I will come upon you." Some interpreters connect this warning to local history: the city's acropolis, trusted as impregnable, had twice been captured by surprise, first by the Persian king Cyrus in the sixth century BC and later by the Greek king Antiochus III, in both cases by soldiers who climbed an unguarded, weathered section of the cliff. Although Sardis was one of the seven churches, excavators have found no church building there from this period.

In the centuries after Revelation was written, Sardis's Temple of Artemis, whose core had stood since the third century BC, gained a partial outer colonnade, though it was never fully finished. The city's grand Bath-Gymnasium complex dates from the late second or early third century AD; one of its halls was later turned into a synagogue, the biggest ancient synagogue yet found.

Today Sardis is an archaeological site near the village of Sart in Türkiye, where excavations continue to uncover the ancient city's acropolis, the Temple of Artemis, and the Roman-era bath and gymnasium complex.

scripture.textWEB: saying, “What you see, write in a book and send to the seven assemblies: to Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and to Laodicea.”

“And to the angel of the assembly in Sardis write: “He who has the seven Spirits of God and the seven stars says these things: “I know your works, that you have a reputation of being alive, but you are dead.
Remember therefore how you have received and heard. Keep it and repent. If therefore you won’t watch, I will come as a thief, and you won’t know what hour I will come upon you.
Nevertheless you have a few names in Sardis that didn’t defile their garments. They will walk with me in white, for they are worthy.
